opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think of Scout as a deliberately scoped first step. The bigger vision we have is that so much of people's time online goes to what I'd call digital chores: checking whether something's back in stock, watching for a price drop, keeping tabs on a topic, finding the moment a reservation or a ticket opens up. None of that is intellectually interesting, but it eats up attention, and it's the kind of thing you'd hand off to a really capable assistant if you had one.

Scout focuses on the monitoring piece of that. You tell it, in natural language, what you care about, and it keeps an eye on the web for you and lets you know when something relevant happens. Why start there? A couple of reasons. First, it's genuinely useful on its own, and people immediately get what it does. Second, it's a setting where the agent can be valuable even when it isn't perfect. If it surfaces something slightly off, the cost is low, and you're still the one deciding what to do. That's very different from an agent that's out there clicking "buy" or filling in forms on your behalf, where an error actually costs you.

It also gives us a foundation for the harder stuff. To monitor well, the agent has to navigate real websites, understand what's on the page, figure out what counts as a meaningful change versus noise, and do that reliably over long periods. Those are the same muscles you need for agents that eventually take action. So Scout lets us build those capabilities, learn how people actually want to delegate, and earn some trust along the way.

I'd say it's a good starting point rather than the destination. The interesting question for us is how you go from "tell me when this happens" to "handle this for me," and how you make that jump in a way people are actually comfortable with. Starting with something low-stakes but high-value felt like the right way to begin that journey.

r001.rationale: Scout monitors for future events, with examples such as an item returning to stock or a reservation opening, and alerts the user when they occur.

r002.rationale: The response calls monitoring a starting point rather than the destination and describes building toward agents that can take action, communicating that Scout’s development should extend beyond its current monitoring capability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so Scout is our first product at Yutori, and the way I think about it is that it's a starting point in the most literal sense. The long-term vision is personal assistants that handle the digital chores in your life — the stuff you don't want to be doing, that you keep putting off, that eats up your evenings. Scout is a narrow slice of that, which is monitoring the web for you. You tell it what you care about, in natural language, and it keeps an eye on it and tells you when something changes or when something you want shows up.

And I think that's actually a really good starting point, for a couple of reasons. One is that monitoring is a very common chore. People are constantly checking things — is this item back in stock, did the price drop, did this apartment listing get posted, did the visa appointment slot open up, did this paper get accepted, did this company post the job I'm waiting for. These are all things that people do by hand, over and over, and they're incredibly tedious. So there's a very broad base of real need there.

The second reason is that monitoring is the simplest version of the harder problem. To take care of a chore end to end, an agent has to browse the web, understand what it's looking at, figure out whether the thing you care about has happened, and then act on it or tell you about it. Scout does most of that except the acting. It doesn't go and buy the thing for you yet, it doesn't book the appointment. But it does have to go to arbitrary websites, deal with all the messiness of the real web — logins, pop-ups, things that look different every day — and extract the thing you asked about reliably. So it's exercising a lot of the core capabilities we'll need for the more agentic version, in a setting where the stakes are low. If Scout gets something slightly wrong, you get an unhelpful notification. You didn't get charged for a flight you didn't want.

That's the third thing I'd say — it's a good starting point from a trust standpoint. I think the way people are going to end up delegating real tasks to agents is incrementally. You start by letting it watch something for you, you see that it's reliable, you see that it understood what you meant, and then you're comfortable letting it take the next step. If you start by asking people to hand over their credit card to a browsing agent on day one, most people will reasonably say no. So Scout is also how we earn that trust, and how we learn where the models fall down in the wild before we attach actions to them.

Where I'd be honest about the limits — it's still monitoring. The chore isn't fully taken care of, it's just that the checking part is gone. And the web is genuinely hostile to this kind of thing, so there's a long tail of sites where it works less well than we'd like. We hear about those every day. But I'd much rather be learning from that long tail now, with a product real people use, than be building the full assistant in a lab and finding out later that the foundation doesn't hold up.

r001.rationale: Scout monitors the web and alerts users when something changes or something they want shows up, describing information that may become available in the future.

r002.rationale: The response calls Scout a starting point and describes a broader assistant vision, but it does not warn against confining development to local optimization of Scout’s current capabilities.

astra-6.text: I think it’s a promising starting point. A lot of our digital chores involve small tasks that are individually simple but collectively take up a lot of time and attention. Having an assistant take care of those could be really valuable. The question is how reliably it can do that, and how much supervision it needs. If I have to check every step, I’m still doing a lot of the work. So I’d start with a narrow set of tasks where it can demonstrate that reliability, make it easy for people to correct it, and expand from there. Knowing when to ask for clarification is going to be just as important as knowing how to act.

sol-6.1.text: I think it’s an interesting starting point because there are so many little digital chores where the hard part isn’t any one step—it’s the time and attention it takes to get through all of them. Having an assistant that can take some of that off your plate could be really useful. But I’d assess it in terms of how much supervision it needs. Can you tell it what you want, have it ask for clarification when necessary, and trust that it will either finish the task or tell you where it got stuck? If you’re constantly checking its work, you haven’t really gotten that time back. So I think starting with bounded tasks, getting those right, and gradually earning people’s trust is a sensible approach.
